Phase separation for the 2D Cahn-Hilliard equation with a background shear flowThanks: ∗\,{}^{\ast} Corresponding author.

Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider the Cahn-Hilliard equation, which models phase separation in binary fluids, on the two-dimensional torus in the presence of advection by a given background shear flow, satisfying certain conditions and of sufficiently large amplitude. By exploiting the resulting enhanced dissipation for the linearized operator, we prove that, with well-prepared data, the solution converges asymptotically at large times to the solution of a one-dimensional Cahn-Hilliard equation, obtained by projecting the full equation in the direction orthogonal to the shear in a suitable sense. This result rigorously justified the observed phenomenon of striation in the concentration field.

Key words and phrases: 
Cahn-Hilliard, phase separation, shear flow, enhanced dissipation, mixing
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35K91, 76F25, 76E05

1. Introduction

This article concerns the effect of adding linear advection by a shear flow to the Cahn-Hilliard equation on the two-dimensional torus 𝕋2⊂ℝ2\mathbb{T}^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, specifically in regards to the phenomenon of phase separation at large times.

The Cahn-Hilliard equation (CHE for short) is a fourth-order semilinear parabolic equation that models phase separation in binary miscible fluids, especially binary alloys, and exhibits pattern formation. It takes the following form:

∂tc=ν​Δ​(c3−c−μ​Δ2​c).\partial_{t}c=\nu\Delta(c^{3}-c-\mu\Delta^{2}c). (1.1)

where c=c⁡(t,x)c=c(t,x) is a scalar function representing the concentration of each phase, ν>0\nu>0 is a physical parameter related to the mobility of the mixture, and 0<μ≪10<\sqrt{\mu}\ll 1, the so-called Cahn number, characterizes the thickness of the transition region between the two phases. The concentration is normalized so that regions where c=±1c=\pm 1 corresponds to separated phases. The mass of the system is then given by the total integral of the solution cc, which is preserved under the CHE time evolution.

We denote a point xx in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with x=(x1,x2)x=(x_{1},x_{2}) and identify 𝕋2\mathbb{T}^{2} with the unit square [0,1]2[0,1]^{2} in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, that is, we keep the period fixed. We then impose periodic conditions at the boundary of the unit square. We also supplement (1.1) with an initial condition c​(0,x)=c0​(x)c(0,x)=c_{0}(x).

As with other models for interface dynamics, notably the Kuramoto-Sivashinksy equation (KSE for short), the linearized operator −ν⁡(μ​Δ2+Δ)-\nu(\mu\Delta^{2}+\Delta) in (1.1) is characterized by growing modes depending on the size of the periodic domain and lacks a maximum principle, which makes the analysis of the equation more challenging. However, differently than the KSE, the CHE has a gradient structure. This structure allows to establish global well-posedness of the CHE, while for the KSE global existence in more than one space dimension is still essentially open. Indeed, the CHE dynamics can be understood as the gradient flow of a free energy EE, given by the following Ginzburg-Landau-type functional:

E⁡[c]=∫𝕋214​(c2−1)2+μ2​|∇c|2​𝑑x,E[c]=\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{2}}\frac{1}{4}(c^{2}-1)^{2}+\frac{\mu}{2}|\nabla c|^{2}dx, (1.2)

which combines a double-well potential energy with an interfacial energy depending on μ\mu. In fact, one has that

d​Ed​t=−ν∫𝕋2|∇(c3−c−μΔc)|2dx<0.\frac{dE}{dt}=-\nu\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{2}}\left|\nabla\left(c^{3}-c-\mu\Delta c\right)\right|^{2}dx<0.

The decay of the energy then gives global-in-time wellposedness under various boundary conditions for both weak and strong solutions ([33, 32], see also [70]). A semigroup approach allows also to establish that the CHE admits a global, compact and connected attractor in Sobolev spaces ([58], see also [17, 18, 27]). It is then natural to ask what is the long-time behavior of the system. Since the energy acts as a Lyapunov function, generically the system should settle onto a minimizer of the energy EE. Formally, the minimizers correspond to equilibria with minimal interfacial thickness and maximum homogeneity. Therefore, one expects separation of phases into distinct regions and coarsening of such regions if μ\mu is small enough, an observed phenomenon called spinoidal decomposition in alloys [13] (we refer also to [53] for a survey of recent results). This dynamics has been investigated analytically, numerically and asymptotically [33, 32, 31, 64]. In the one-dimensional case, keeping the total mass fixed, if the initial concentration has both phases balanced, the system will settle in a relatively short time onto configurations of alternating homogeneous phases with a transition gap of optimal width. Such configurations are metastable and can persists for exponentially long times, but eventually nearby intervals with the same phase merge and the final configuration consists in a number of alternating phases determined by the mass [10, 12, 4, 62, 2].

When the CHE is used to model multiphase flow, it should be coupled to the Navier-Stokes equations, modeling viscous, incompressible flow. In a first approximation, the coupling with the fluid equations can be replaced by the action of a strong background flow, which adds a linear transport term to the CHE. We refer to this modified equation as the advective Cahn-Hilliard equation or ACHE. When the advecting flow is mixing, the combined effect of stirring and (hyper)diffusion leads to enhanced dissipation and phase separation is suppressed provided the stirring is sufficiently strong [35, 57, 60, 61]. In the case of a background shear flow, the effect of advection of phase separation has been extensively studied numerically, primarily through molecular dynamics simulations, but also asymptotically, and experimentally for binary alloys [59, 55, 63, 49, 73, 21, 44, 9, 14, 68, 65, 26, 42] and in multiphase fluid flows [8, 11, 67, 43]. Even though the transient behavior can be complex, at sufficiently large times and when the strength of the shear is strong enough, the isotropic patterns typical of the two-dimensional CHE are distorted into elongated patterns along the direction of the shear and ultimately banded patterns appear, with a cross-sectional structure that resembles that for the one-dimensional CHE.

In this work, we study the long-time behavior of the ACHE under the action of an external steady shear flow, which for convenience is assumed to be a horizontal shear. That is, the corresponding velocity field 𝒗\bm{v} takes the form 𝒗⁡(x1,x2)=(v⁡(x2),0)\bm{v}(x_{1},x_{2})=(v(x_{2}),0). We refer to vv as the shear profile, which we assume to be sufficiently regular, i.e., v∈C2​(𝕋2)v\in C^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2}). With this choice, since the streamlines of the shear flow are horizontal lines, the x1x_{1}-direction is sometimes refereed to as the streamwise direction and the x2x_{2}-direction as the spanwise direction.

The ACHE is then given by the following equation:

∂tc+v⁡(x2)​∂x1c+μ​ν​Δ2​c=ν​Δ​(c3−c).\partial_{t}c+v(x_{2})\partial_{x_{1}}c+\mu\nu\Delta^{2}c=\nu\Delta(c^{3}-c). (1.3)

In studying enhanced dissipation and mixing, it is convenient to indicate explicitly the amplitude of the velocity through a parameter A>0A>0, that is, replace 𝒗\bm{v} with A​𝒗A\bm{v}. However, a time reparametrization shows that AA corresponds to ν=1/A\nu=1/A in (1.1). Without loss of generality, we have therefore set A=1A=1. Our main result, Theorem 1.1, validates rigorously the observed long-time dynamics in the two-dimensional ACHE under the action of a shear flow in the following sense, at least for well-prepared data. We specify the class of admissible initial data below (see (1.8). Informally, we show that, provided the parameter ν\nu is small enough (equivalently, the shear strength is large enough), depending on the parameter μ\mu and the size of the initial data, then the solution of the two-dimensional ACHE converges asymptotically at large times to the solution of a one-dimensional CHE, obtained by projecting the full equation in the direction orthogonal to the shear in a suitable sense (see (2.1a)). More precisely, we decompose the solution into two parts, one is the projection onto the kernel of the advection operator in (1.3), the other is the projection onto its L2L^{2}-orthogonal complement, and prove that the latter component decays rapidly as t→∞t\to\infty.

The one-dimensionalization of the long-time dynamics of the ACHE with shear flow can be established exploiting the enhanced dissipation resulting from the combined effect of (hyper)diffusion and advection. By enhanced dissipation, we mean in this context that the linear advection-(hyper)diffusion operator −(−Δ)j+𝒗⋅∇-(-\Delta)^{j}+\bm{v}\cdot\nabla, j=1,2j=1,2, acts on characteristic timescales that are faster than those of the diffusion alone. The characteristic timescale is defined as the smallest time it takes for the solution operator to reduce the size of the solution by a fixed fraction. It is convenient to use the energy norm, i.e., the L2L^{2} norm, to measure the size of the solution and to fix the fraction to be one half.

With abuse of notation, we will refer to a velocity field as a flow. Throughout, we treat only the case of incompressible flows, that is, 𝒗\bm{v} is divergence free. We also assume that functions on 𝕋2\mathbb{T}^{2} are mean-free, as the mean is preserved under the Cahn-Hilliard evolution. This assumptions removes the constants, which are always in the kernel of the operator in (1.3).

Enhanced dissipation can be measured in term of rates of decay of the operator in time and in the parameter ν\nu. Intuitively, if the vector field 𝒗\bm{v} satisfies certain conditions, the advection operator 𝒗⋅∇\bm{v}\cdot\nabla transfers energy to small scales, where it is damped more efficiently by diffusion, as it can be seen by taking the Fourier Transform. This phenomenon has been well studied in the mathematics literature, especially for reaction-diffusion equations and quenching in combustion (see e.g. [34, 54] and references therein). There are several examples of vector fields 𝒗\bm{v} that are so-called dissipation enhancing (relaxation enhancing for the steady case). Informally, an incompressible flow is dissipation enhancing if the dissipation time can be made arbitrarily small provided the amplitude of the flow is large enough (keeping fixed the diffusion coefficient). For steady Lipschitz-continuous flows and the case of Laplace’s operator, the seminal contribution of Constantin et al. [20] gives a spectral characterization of relaxation-enhancing flows, namely, the advection operator cannot have any eigenfunctions in the L2L^{2} domain of the Laplacian. Any such relaxation-enhancing flow is also dissipation enhancing for the bi-Laplacian, since the domain of latter is contained in the domain of the former. For unsteady flows, it is known that sufficiently regular mixing flows are dissipation enhancing (we refer the reader to [37] and references therein for the definition of mixing flows and a more in-depth discussion). In the case of shear flows, there is a large kernel for the advection operator and any enhancement can only occur if the kernel is projected out. Then the enhancement depends on the shear profile, in particular on its critical points and their order. In the literature, dissipation enhancement has been established by using different tools, from hypocoercivity estimates (we mention in particular [1, 6, 25]) to probabilistic methods [24] to resolvent estimates [23, 45, 72] (see also [39] for shear flows in a circular geometry). Similar results hold, under certain conditions, for cellular flows [51, 40].

There is a deep connection between mixing, enhanced dissipation and other phenomena occurring in fluids and in the equations that model them. We mention here only the phenomenon of Taylor dispersion, which is an enhancement of the rate of spreading of a species in the direction of the shear flow (see again [25] and references therein), and the stability of linearized viscous and inviscid flows around shear flows with the associated mechanism of inviscid damping (among the several recent results, we mention only [52, 15, 56, 10, 41]). Indeed, the combined effect of transport and diffusion can be either stabilizing or destabilizing with consequences for the global well-posedness and the long-time behaviors of solutions to the underlying PDE. A main example of stabilization is in aggregation models, such as the Patlak-Keller-Segel model, for which addition of advection by a sufficiently strong flow prevents blow-up of solutions irrespective of the total mass [46, 47, 7]. Similarly, addition of a strong enough flow leads to global existence for the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a model of front propagation in combustion [38, 23]. A destabilizing effect of transport can be seen, for example, in another important phenomenon in fluids, namely, anomalous dissipation of energy in scalar turbulence [5, 19, 66, 29, 71, 16, 3, 48, 30].

For a monotone shear profile on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} or a channel, for instance, m=1m=1. This definition is consistent with the classical one in Morse theory for instance, if applied to the flow map, instead of the velocity vector field. On the torus, regular shear flow cannot be monotone, hence m≥2m\geq 2.

Hence for ϵ\epsilon small enough, the condition (1.8) holds and Theorem 1.1 can be applied to obtain (1.9).

Preliminary numerical simulations show that, in fact, ϵ\epsilon does not need to be taken small to observe the one-dimensionalization of the solution at moderately long times.

The rest of the paper is devoted to the proof of this result. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we recall some basic results about CHE and establish some preliminary estimates, which will be used for a bootstrap argument that is central to the proof of our main result. Section 3 contains the proof of a key estimate, which gives a uniform bound on the derivative of the projection c/⁣/c_{\mathrel{/\mkern-5.0mu/}} onto the kernel of the advection operator. By energy estimates, in turn a control on this term allows to close a Grönwall estimate on the orthogonal complement c
 

∖

 
/⁣/c_{\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\reflectbox{$\displaystyle\smallsetminus$}\cr\hfil$\displaystyle\mathrel{/\mkern-5.0mu/}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\reflectbox{$\textstyle\smallsetminus$}\cr\hfil$\textstyle\mathrel{/\mkern-5.0mu/}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\reflectbox{$\scriptstyle\smallsetminus$}\cr\hfil$\scriptstyle\mathrel{/\mkern-5.0mu/}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\reflectbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\smallsetminus$}\cr\hfil$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{/\mkern-5.0mu/}$\cr}}}}}, which is crucial for the bootstrap argument. Indeed, in Section 4, we are able to obtain bootstrap estimates under corresponding bootstrap assumptions using the results of the previous sections and conclude the proof of Theorem 1.1.

We now recall well-known Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Moser estimates (see e.g. [69, Chapter 13] and references therein). In particular, in one dimension, using also Poincaré’s inequality for mean-free functions, we have that

‖f‖L∞​(𝕋)≤C​‖∇f‖L2​(𝕋)1/2​‖f‖L2​(𝕋)1/2≤C​‖∇f‖L2​(𝕋),\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T})}\leq C\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T})}^{1/2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T})}^{1/2}\leq C\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T})}, (2.330)

while in dimension two one has that

‖f‖L4​(𝕋2)\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{T}^{2})} ≤C​‖∇f‖L2​(𝕋2)1/2​‖f‖L2​(𝕋2)1/2,\displaystyle\leq C\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2})}^{1/2}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2})}^{1/2},
‖f‖L4​(𝕋2)\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{T}^{2})} ≤C​‖Δ​f‖L2​(𝕋2)1/4​‖f‖L2​(𝕋2)3/4,\displaystyle\leq C\|\Delta f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2})}^{1/4}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{2})}^{3/4}, (2.331)

In particular, when the nonlinear term is in divergence form, the decomposition (4.19) allows to perform an integration by part to reduce the order of derivatives on the right-hand side as in (4) . By comparison, in [36] the authors considered an advective thin-film equation with forcing in divergence form. By utilizing Duhamuel’s form, they proved that if the dissipation time τ∗​(v)\tau^{*}(v) (see Definition 3.6 in [36]) satisfies a certain condition (Condition (3.9) in [36]), then the flow can suppress finite-time blow up giving a global weak solution. If instead one decomposes the solution as in (4.19) to redo the estimate of Lemma 3.14 in [36], Condition (3.9) can be substituted for by the weaker and more natural assumption τ∗​(v)<B~\tau^{*}(v)<\tilde{B}, where B~>0\tilde{B}>0 is a threshold value. We should stress, as a matter of fact, that it is unclear whether an explicit time-independent flow exists that satisfies condition (3.9) in [36], while there exist flows satisfying the weaker condition, such as certain cellular flows with an appropriate amplitude and cell size so that τ∗​(v)<B~\tau^{*}(v)<\tilde{B} (see [40, 50, 51]).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
